entry.title: Putting It All Together: A Complete Next.js Mini-Agent Project Recap and Full Integration Guide
entry.summary: Following our guide on Client Components vs. Server Components in a Next.js AI agent, this post completes our 14-part Next.js implementation module by assembling DevPulse into a single cohesive application. When an agent proposes a state-changing action (such as drafting a bug ticket via draftIssueTicket), clicking the confirmation button in React must trigger an idempotent server mutation rather than only toggling local UI state. By using upsert with onConflict: 'tool_call_id' in our approveAndPersistTicket Server Action, double-clicks never create duplicate tickets in Supabase. When navigating between sessions via query params, always key the client chat component with key={activeSessionKey} in page.tsx so React cleanly resets local hooks (useSmartAutoScroll, approvedTickets, and useChat) for the new session. entry.title: CVE-2026-119618: Apache HTTP/2 Pre-Auth RCE — What the Race Condition Actually Does
entry.summary: There is a CVSS 9.8 pre-authentication remote code execution vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server’s mod_http2 module. It was fixed on 11 November 2026 in version 2.4.71. If you run Apache with HTTP/2 enabled and you have not patched, this post is for you. What happens mod_http2 is designed so that worker threads never touch the connection’s shared allocator — each worker gets a private one. assign_headers() breaks that rule for a specific request shape: body-less, with Content-Type and no Content-Length, when the request header table is full. The worker writes a synthesised Content-Length: 0 into the shared stream table. That write races with the connection thread on a lock-free free list. Two threads pop the same node. Heap corrupts. The process ends up with double-owned memory, and that’s the primitive the exploit turns into code execution. No credentials. No user interaction. The attacker sends an HTTP/2 request. Who’s affected Apache HTTP Server 2.4.55 through 2.4.70, and standalone mod_h2 2.0.8 through 2.0.42 — but only if HTTP/2 is enabled. That’s the h2 or h2c token in the Protocols directive. The directive can be set server-wide or per virtual host, so check both. Scale Wiz reports 64% of cloud environments have resources on a vulnerable version, and 51% have publicly exposed instances. A containerised differential lab, ThreadSanitizer evidence, and a stdlib HTTP/2 PoC are already on GitHub under the CVE identifier. Fix Upgrade to Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 or mod_h2 2.0.43. RHEL 9: mod_http2-2.0.26-7.el9_9.1. RHEL 10: mod_http2-2.0.29-5.el10_3.1. Container images built before 11 November need a rebuild. If you can’t patch today: Protocols http/1.1 in every config file and every virtual host block. Full write-up with hunt guidance and Red Hat vs upstream rating breakdown: https://threataft.com/articles/cve-2026-119618-apache-mod-http2-race-condition-rce

entry.title: Set up F1 print-status lights on a Klipper printer in 30 minutes
entry.summary:
My Voron's LED strip changes colour with the print: blue when idle, orange heating, white printing, green chequered flag when it's done, red for errors. It's WLED_Voron--F1-Lights, and it now has a setup guide that GitHub checks every week. Not Klipper itself. But it can check the bits people actually get wrong:
all eight LED_* macros exist and every value is in range the guide's one-line sed really does change all nine IP addresses (there's no single variable for it, which is the most annoying part of the setup) the optional print macros only call macros that exist each macro's numbers arrive at a fake WLED as valid JSON with the right colour, brightness and effect a strip that's switched off can't hang a print: the script gives up in about 3 seconds Most WS2812B and COB strips are GRB, so red and green arrive swapped. The defaults are written for that: heating sends 80 255 0 to get orange. If your WLED colour order is already set to match the strip, heating comes out green and errors come out... also green. The guide says exactly which three lines to swap.
Flash WLED, install gcode_shell_command, copy the script and wled.cfg, change the nine addresses, [include wled.cfg], restart, and type LED_IDLE in the console. Full steps, with the Moonraker bit and every error I've hit: docs/SETUP.md. Based on Gliptopolis/WLED_Klipper, reworked on my Voron 2. What colours would you use for a failed print, red or something more dramatic? 🤖 Drafted with AI assistance from my own homelab notes, logs and repos, then reviewed and edited before publishing.

entry.title: You Watched Five People Try Your Feature and Most of Them Could Not Find It
entry.summary: Your team finally ran a usability session. Five people from outside the team were asked to complete a task using the new feature you built, while you watched quietly on a call. Three of them never found the button. One found it and then did not trust what it did. Only one finished without help. You spent six weeks on that feature. Watching it fail in silence is one of the hardest kinds of feedback to receive, because nobody is saying anything critical. They are just struggling, and you cannot help. That is exactly why it is so valuable. Every other kind of feedback on your work is somebody's opinion. This is behaviour. Nobody was being polite, nobody was guessing what users might do, and nobody had read the design document first. Resist the first reaction, which is to explain. They should have looked at the menu. They were not our target users. The tooltip covers it. Some of that may be true, but if three people out of five missed it, the next three hundred will as well. The usability researcher Jakob Nielsen has long argued that a handful of test users finds most of the obvious problems, which is why five people can tell you so much. Instead, go back through the recordings or your notes and write down the exact moments people hesitated. Where did their mouse go first? What did they say out loud while they looked? Which words on the screen did they read, and which did they skip? Those moments are your list of fixes, and they are far more precise than anything a reviewer could have written. Then separate the problems from the solutions. Users are excellent at showing you where something is wrong and much less reliable at telling you how to fix it. If one participant says just make the button red, note that they could not see it, and then decide with your designer how to make it findable. Finally, thank the team for running the session, and ask to watch the next one before you build anything. The cheapest time to learn this lesson is before six weeks of work. – Asael Shinder

entry.title: A, CNAME, MX, TXT : à quoi sert vraiment chaque enregistrement DNS
entry.summary:
Ouvrir la zone DNS de son domaine pour la première fois, c'est tomber sur un tableau de sigles sans explication. En réalité il n'y a que quatre lignes à comprendre, et elles suffisent pour 95 % des situations. C'est l'enregistrement de base. Il associe un nom à une adresse IP. creebs.fr. 3600 IN A 109.234.165.64
À lire ainsi : le nom creebs.fr mène à la machine 109.234.165.64, et cette information est valable 3600 secondes. Son équivalent pour les adresses modernes est AAAA, qui fait la même chose avec une adresse IPv6. Si votre hébergeur en fournit une, mettez les deux. Un CNAME ne pointe pas vers une machine mais vers un autre nom, qui sera résolu à son tour. www.creebs.fr. 3600 IN CNAME creebs.fr.
L'intérêt est l'entretien : le jour où vous changez de ser…
